draft.title: Sentence patterns for effect
card: Short sentences
A short sentence reads fast and stops suddenly. Writers use it to build tension or to deliver a shock. Example: "The door creaked. Then the lights died."
Long sentences
A long, flowing sentence carries the reader along and slows the pace. It can create a calm, dreamy or drawn-out mood. Example: "We drifted down the slow brown river, warmed by the sun."
Repeated patterns
When a writer repeats the same sentence pattern, the repetition builds emphasis. Example: "We were tired. We were hungry. We kept going."
To name the effect, look at the length or pattern of the sentences, then say what it does to the reader's pace and feelings.
draft.remember: Sentence length and pattern shape the pace and feeling: short for tension or shock, long for a slow pace, repeated for emphasis.

a.q: Which choice is most likely to build sudden tension?
opts: Footsteps stopped. A handle turned
The footsteps drifted slowly along the hallway to us
Down the long hall, past the clock, came footsteps
The footsteps were slow, and the hallway was quiet
a.why: Two very short sentences read quickly and stop sharply, which builds tension. The longer sentences slow the pace and read more smoothly, so they do not create the same sudden effect.
a.clue: Which option reads fastest and stops abruptly?

b.q: Mia writes: "I wanted to win. I wanted to run faster. I wanted a cheer." What is the main effect of the repeated sentence pattern?
opts: It builds emphasis on how strongly she wants to win
It slows the pace to create a calm, dreamy mood
It shocks the reader with a sudden surprise
It shows the narrator is unsure about what she wants
b.why: Repeating "I wanted" three times stresses how strong her desire is. The sentences are short, but the effect comes from the repeated pattern, not from a slow pace or a sudden shock.
b.clue: Look at how each sentence begins, not only at its length.
